newsitem.title: USA: Brazil Central Bank wants exports to cut trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Central Bank wants exports to cut trade gap.

text.p: Brazil wants to cut its widening trade deficit through increased exports rather than the use of import controls, Central Bank International Affairs Director Gustavo Franco said on Tuesday.
Franco told Reuters Financial Television that a rapid devaluation of Brazil's currency, the real, was not a way to increase exports.
"I don't forecast any major change in the rhythm with which the real has been changing that would make any difference," he said.

Brazilian officials on Tuesday reported a $2.03 billion trade deficit in the first two months of 1997. The figure was within expectations but in sharp contrast to the $13 million surplus in the same period last year.
Some analysts have predicted Brazil could see a $10 billion trade deficit for the year, up from $5.5 billion last year.
Asked if he considered the $10 billion figure alarmist, Franco said, "I think so. It looks like too much."
Franco, one of the architects of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's two-and-a-half-year-old economic stabilization plan, rejected import controls to cut the gap.
"We wouldn't like to compromise by any means the experiment of trade liberalization we've conducted in Brazil since July 1994," when the plan was launched.
"The benefits of having an open trading regime are enormous ... we wouldn't like to sacrifice that."
He added, "So the place to attack is exporting. We are confident we have built the right fundamentals for having good export components."
Franco, who was in New York to attend conferences, said the January and February trade deficit had been artificially worsened in part by the start of a new system of import registration.
Brazil usually also sees higher exports in the months from March to October. The trade surplus for January and February 1996 could have been helped by a mild recession, he said.
"The specifics of how to attack the problem will of course be defined by the specifics of the problem. We have to look in to the figures and see what's going on," he said.
